topics.summary: Sectors and segments, minor and major

content.text:
You have already come across the terms sector and segment of a circle in your earlier classes. Recall that the portion (or part) of the circular region enclosed by two radii and the corresponding arc is called a sector of the circle and the portion (or part) of the circular region enclosed between a chord and the corresponding arc is called a segment of the circle.

Thus, in the figure, shaded region OAPB is a sector of the circle with centre O. ∠ AOB is called the angle of the sector. Note that in this figure, unshaded region OAQB is also a sector of the circle. For obvious reasons, OAPB is called the minor sector and OAQB is called the major sector. You can also see that angle of the major sector is 360° - ∠ AOB.

Now, look at the next figure, in which AB is a chord of the circle with centre O. So, shaded region APB is a segment of the circle. You can also note that unshaded region AQB is another segment of the circle formed by the chord AB. For obvious reasons, APB is called the minor segment and AQB is called the major segment.

concepts.concept_name: The area of a sector: try it first

content.text:
In a way, we can consider this circular region to be a sector forming an angle of 360° (i.e., of degree measure 360) at the centre O. Now by applying the Unitary Method, we can arrive at the area of the sector OAPB as follows:

When degree measure of the angle at the centre is 360, area of the sector = πr²

So, when the degree measure of the angle at the centre is 1, area of the sector = πr² / 360

Therefore, when the degree measure of the angle at the centre is θ, area of the sector = (πr² / 360) × θ = (θ/360) × πr².

Thus, we obtain the following relation (or formula) for area of a sector of a circle:

Area of the sector of angle θ = (θ/360) × πr²,

where r is the radius of the circle and θ the angle of the sector in degrees.

topics.summary: The length of an arc of a sector

content.text:
Now, a natural question arises : Can we find the length of the arc APB corresponding to this sector? Yes. Again, by applying the Unitary Method and taking the whole length of the circle (of angle 360°) as 2πr, we can obtain the required length of the arc APB as (θ/360) × 2πr.

So, length of an arc of a sector of angle θ = (θ/360) × 2πr.

= 46.1 cm² (approx.)

For finding the area of Δ OAB, draw OM ⊥ AB as shown in the figure.
Note that OA = OB. Therefore, by RHS congruence, Δ AMO ≅ Δ BMO.
So, M is the mid-point of AB and ∠ AOM = ∠ BOM = (1/2) × 120° = 60°.

Let OM = x cm
So, from Δ OMA, OM / OA = cos 60°
or, x / 21 = 1/2    [cos 60° = 1/2]
or, x = 21/2
So, OM = 21/2 cm

Also, AM / OA = sin 60° = √3 / 2
So, AM = (21√3) / 2 cm
Therefore, AB = 2 AM = 2 × (21√3)/2 cm = 21√3 cm

So, area of Δ OAB = (1/2) × AB × OM = (1/2) × 21√3 × (21/2) cm²
= (441√3) / 4 cm²    (3)

Therefore, area of the segment AYB = (462 - (441√3)/4) cm²    [From (1), (2) and (3)]
= (21/4) (88 - 21√3) cm²

Determine the central angle from indirect data such as elapsed time on a clock or a right angle subtended by a chord.

Determine when to use right-triangle methods versus sin/cos methods for the inscribed triangle's area in a segment.

media.title: 60-Second Recap of Areas Related to Circles
media.description: A 90-second concise recap. The (θ/360) factor is highlighted, then applied first to 2πr (giving arc length) and then to πr² (giving sector area). The segment formula appears as 'sector minus triangle', illustrated by a slide-out triangle. Major identities close out.
media.teaching_notes: Play as the very last activity. Pause at 65s and ask the student to predict why the segment formula reuses the sector area - attempt-before-reveal. After the video, ask the student to write all three formulas from memory.

The fraction (θ/360) is highlighted in Orange and floats above the circle. On-screen text: 'A single fraction governs every formula in this chapter.'. Scene 2 (15-35s): The arc highlighted in Orange. The arc length formula '(θ/360) × 2πr' slides in beside the circle in Orange. Scene 3 (35-55s): The sector shaded Light Blue. The sector area formula '(θ/360) × πr²' slides in below the arc length formula. The (θ/360) factor in both formulas is highlighted in matching Orange so the student sees the SAME factor. Scene 4 (55-70s): The segment formula scene - the triangle slides out of the sector, leaving the segment behind. The formula 'Segment area = sector area - triangle area' slides in below the previous two. Pause at 65s with on-screen prompt: 'Why does the segment formula use the sector area as one of its parts?'. Scene 5 (70-90s): The major-region identities appear in two boxes: 'Major sector = πr² - minor sector' and 'Major segment = πr² - minor segment' in Dark Green. Final shot: all three formulas + two identities visible at once with the central (θ/360) factor still glowing Orange. Visual elements: 5-color palette (Navy Blue, Orange, Light Blue, Dark Green, Black). No music; on-screen text only.
media.instructions_for_student: Watch the recap. Then close the video and try to write all three formulas on paper from memory. Use the major-region identities for any major-area question on revision.

11.1 Areas of Sector and Segment of a Circle

HOOK: A friend orders a 12-inch pizza for a class party and asks the shop to cut it into 8 equal slices. Each slice runs from the centre of the pizza to its crust along two straight cuts and one curved edge. If, instead, a single straight cut is made across the pizza along a chord that does not pass through the centre, the smaller piece left on one side of the cut is bounded by that straight chord and a curved arc. These two everyday pieces - the wedge-shaped slice and the chord-bounded crust piece - are exactly what we will name in this chapter as the sector and the segment of a circle.

RECALL: You have already come across the terms sector and segment of a circle in your earlier classes. Recall that the portion (or part) of the circular region enclosed by two radii and the corresponding arc is called a sector of the circle, and the portion (or part) of the circular region enclosed between a chord and the corresponding arc is called a segment of the circle.

CORE - Sector:
Thus, in Fig. 11.1, shaded region OAPB is a sector of the circle with centre O. ∠ AOB is called the angle of the sector. Note that in this figure, unshaded region OAQB is also a sector of the circle. The same circle therefore has TWO sectors at any chord-free split: a smaller one and a larger one. For obvious reasons, OAPB is called the minor sector and OAQB is called the major sector. You can also see that the angle of the major sector is 360° - ∠ AOB - because the two sector angles together must complete the full 360° of the circle.

CORE - Segment:
Now, look at Fig. 11.2 in which AB is a chord of the circle with centre O. So, shaded region APB is a segment of the circle. You can also note that unshaded region AQB is another segment of the circle formed by the same chord AB. For obvious reasons, APB is called the minor segment and AQB is called the major segment. Notice that the chord AB does the splitting here, not the radii.

ERROR ALERT: A common confusion at this stage is to think that ‘minor’ and ‘major’ refer to whichever piece you happen to colour first. The correct rule is geometric: the minor sector is the one whose central angle is less than 180° (or, equivalently, the smaller of the two pieces), and the major sector is the other one. The same logic, applied to a chord instead of two radii, decides minor and major segments. Two pieces, one decided by central angle, the other by chord-cut size.

WHY THIS STEP? Because keeping minor versus major straight depends on remembering WHAT does the splitting (two radii for a sector, one chord for a segment), not on a vague sense of ‘smallness’.

Remark : When we write ‘segment’ and ‘sector’ we will mean the ‘minor segment’ and the ‘minor sector’ respectively, unless stated otherwise. This convention will simplify almost every formula and example in the chapter.

CHECK: Imagine the same pizza of radius 15 cm. (a) If the cook makes one cut from the centre to the crust and a second cut also from the centre, what kind of region is enclosed between the two cuts and the curved crust - a sector or a segment? (b) If, instead, the cook makes one straight cut across the pizza without going through the centre, what kind of region is the smaller piece on one side of that cut? (c) For each case, what extra information would you need to label the piece as ‘minor’?

carried_over_topics.summary: This topic builds the area-of-sector formula from the full disc area πr² using the unitary method. Treating the full circle as a sector of central angle 360°, the area corresponding to an angle of 1° is πr²/360, and the area corresponding to a central angle of θ° is therefore (θ/360) × πr². For example, a sector of a circle with radius 14 cm and central angle 60° has area (60/360) × (22/7) × 14 × 14 ≈ 102.7 cm² (with π = 22/7). The formula applies to ANY sector of any circle whose central angle is given in degrees - a single tool for the entire chapter.

carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: For Diwali, a student draws a circular rangoli of radius 14 cm and decides to colour just one decorative wedge running from the centre to the boundary, spanning 60°. To know exactly how much coloured rice powder is needed, she has to compute the area of that one wedge - a sector of a 14 cm circle with central angle 60°. By the end of this topic you will be able to do that calculation, and the same calculation, for any sector at all.

RECALL: We already named the sector of a circle as the wedge-shaped region cut off by two radii and the arc between them. Now with this knowledge, let us try to find some relations (or formulae) to calculate their areas.

CORE - Setting up the unitary method:
Let OAPB be a sector of a circle with centre O and radius r (see Fig. 11.3). Let the degree measure of ∠ AOB be θ. You know that the area of a circle (in fact of a circular region or disc) is πr². In a way, we can consider this entire circular region to be a sector forming an angle of 360° (i.e., of degree measure 360) at the centre O. Now by applying the Unitary Method, we can arrive at the area of the sector OAPB as follows:

When degree measure of the angle at the centre is 360, area of the sector = πr²
So, when the degree measure of the angle at the centre is 1, area of the sector = πr² / 360
Therefore, when the degree measure of the angle at the centre is θ, area of the sector = (πr² / 360) × θ = (θ/360) × πr².

WHY THIS STEP? The unitary method works because the area scales linearly with the central angle: doubling θ doubles the slice, halving θ halves it. So once we know what 1° is worth, we just multiply by however many degrees the sector actually has.

Thus, we obtain the following relation (or formula) for area of a sector of a circle:

Area of the sector of angle θ = (θ/360) × πr²,

where r is the radius of the circle and θ the angle of the sector in degrees.

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 (complete) - Diwali rangoli wedge:
For the rangoli of radius 14 cm with a coloured wedge of central angle 60°, take π = 22/7.
Step 1: Identify the formula → Area = (θ/360) × πr².
Step 2: Substitute θ = 60, r = 14, π = 22/7.
Step 3: Area = (60/360) × (22/7) × 14 × 14 cm² = (1/6) × (22/7) × 196 cm².
Step 4: Simplify → (22 × 196) / (6 × 7) = 4312 / 42 ≈ 102.67 cm².
So about 103 cm² of coloured powder fills that single 60° wedge.

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 (partially faded) - a 90° wedge of the same rangoli:
Step 1: Area = (θ/360) × πr² with θ = 90, r = 14.
Step 2: Area = (90/360) × (22/7) × 196 cm².
Step 3 (you complete): Simplify (90/360) to 1/4 and finish the calculation. Does your answer come out to exactly 1.5 × the 60° wedge area? Why or why not?

ERROR ALERT: A frequent mistake is to multiply just θ × πr² and forget to divide by 360. That treats every sector as if it were the whole circle, which would say a 60° wedge has 60 times the area of the full disc - clearly wrong. Another trap: writing θ in radians (like π/3 for 60°). The formula (θ/360) × πr² expects θ in DEGREES; using radians silently breaks it.

CHECK: A friend says, ‘For a sector of angle 120° in a circle of radius 21 cm, with π = 22/7, the area is (120/360) × (22/7) × 21 × 21 cm².’ Carry out the simplification and state the final area in cm². Then explain in one sentence why the answer must be exactly one-third of πr² for this circle.

carried_over_topics.summary: This topic gives the matching length formula for an arc subtending a central angle θ. Because the full circle has perimeter 2πr and central angle 360°, the arc subtending angle θ has length (θ/360) × 2πr - the same fraction (θ/360) that scales the sector area. For example, on a circular cricket boundary of radius 70 m, an arc subtending 30° at the centre has length (30/360) × 2 × (22/7) × 70 ≈ 36.7 m. Arc length is always larger than the corresponding chord (except in the trivial θ = 0° case).

carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: At a cricket ground with a circular boundary of radius 70 m, a fielder watches the ball roll along the boundary line from one position to another. If the line joining the two positions to the centre of the pitch makes an angle of 30°, the ball travels along an arc subtending 30° at the centre. To know how many metres the chasing fielder must sprint, we need not the chord straight across, but the curved arc length itself.

RECALL: You have just seen that the area of a sector of angle θ is (θ/360) × πr² - a fraction (θ/360) of the full disc area πr². The same fraction logic will now give the arc length.

CORE - Unitary method, again:
Now, a natural question arises : Can we find the length of the arc APB corresponding to this sector? Yes. Again, by applying the Unitary Method and taking the whole length of the circle (of angle 360°) as 2πr, we can obtain the required length of the arc APB as (θ/360) × 2πr.

So, length of an arc of a sector of angle θ = (θ/360) × 2πr.

WHY THIS STEP? The whole circle has length 2πr and central angle 360°. An arc with central angle θ takes the SAME fraction of that perimeter as its sector took of the area - one formula, two uses.

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 (complete) - Cricket boundary arc:
For r = 70 m and θ = 30°, take π = 22/7.
Step 1: Arc length = (θ/360) × 2πr = (30/360) × 2 × (22/7) × 70 m.
Step 2: Simplify 30/360 = 1/12; 2 × (22/7) × 70 = 440 m (the full perimeter).
Step 3: Arc length = (1/12) × 440 m = 36.67 m (approx.).
So the chasing fielder must cover roughly 36.7 m of curved boundary.

ERROR ALERT: A common confusion is to mix up arc length and chord length. The chord is the straight line from A to B; the arc is the curve. They are equal only when θ = 0° (which gives no piece at all). For every other θ, the arc is longer than the chord. Another slip is to use the area formula with 2πr in place of πr², or vice versa - the units already warn you (m² versus m).

CHECK: For the same cricket ground with r = 70 m, what is the arc length when θ = 90°? Should it be exactly one-quarter of the full boundary 2πr? Verify by direct substitution.

carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: Recall the pizza scenario from earlier in this section. If the cook makes one straight cut across a pizza along a chord that does not pass through the centre, the smaller piece left on one side is a segment of the circle. To know its area - say, to estimate cheese coverage - you cannot directly use the sector formula. The piece is bounded by a chord and an arc, not by two radii. You need a method that combines what you already know.

RECALL: In the previous topic you derived the area of a sector as (θ/360) × πr². We will now build on that, plus the well-known formula for the area of a triangle, to reach the segment area.

CORE - Decomposition:
Now let us take the case of the area of the segment APB of a circle with centre O and radius r (see Fig. 11.4). You can see that:

Area of the segment APB = Area of the sector OAPB - Area of Δ OAB
                       = (θ/360) × πr² - area of Δ OAB

WHY THIS STEP? The minor sector OAPB is exactly the minor segment APB plus the triangle OAB, glued along the chord AB. Subtracting the triangle from the sector therefore strips away the radial part and leaves the chord-bounded segment alone.

Note : From Fig. 11.3 and Fig. 11.4 respectively, you can observe that:

Area of the major sector OAQB = πr² - Area of the minor sector OAPB
and            Area of major segment AQB = πr² - Area of the minor segment APB

These two ‘major = full disc minus minor’ identities are very handy. Whenever the question asks for a major region, compute the corresponding minor region first and subtract from πr².

ERROR ALERT: A frequent mistake is to forget the triangle subtraction altogether and report the sector area as the segment area. Another is to subtract the WRONG triangle - some students subtract the area of the larger triangle that the chord forms with a different point on the circle. The triangle is always Δ OAB with O the centre and A, B the chord’s endpoints - an isosceles triangle with two sides equal to r.

CHECK: For a circle of radius 10 cm, suppose a chord AB subtends a 90° angle at the centre. Without computing the segment area yet, write down: (a) the area of the corresponding minor sector, (b) the area of triangle OAB (its legs are both 10 cm), and (c) what subtraction would give you the area of the minor segment.

carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: We now put the sector area formula to work on a textbook problem. The same wedge-area calculation that sized the Diwali rangoli wedge will now answer two related questions at once - the area of a small wedge AND the area of the much larger remaining wedge of the same circle.

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 (complete):
Example 1 : Find the area of the sector of a circle with radius 4 cm and of angle 30°. Also, find the area of the corresponding major sector (Use π = 3.14).

Solution : Given sector is OAPB (see Fig. 11.5).

Step 1 - Set up the formula:
Area of the sector = (θ/360) × πr²

Step 2 - Substitute θ = 30, r = 4, π = 3.14:
Area = (30/360) × 3.14 × 4 × 4 cm²

Step 3 - Simplify the fraction (30/360) = 1/12, and 3.14 × 16 = 50.24:
Area = (50.24 / 12) cm² = (12.56 / 3) cm² = 4.19 cm² (approx.)

WHY THIS STEP? We chose to simplify in fractional form first so that the rounding happens only at the very last step. Rounding too early in a multi-step calculation lets small errors compound.

Method A - ‘Subtract from the whole disc’ for the major sector:
Area of the corresponding major sector
= πr² - area of sector OAPB
= (3.14 × 16 - 4.19) cm²
= 46.05 cm² = 46.1 cm² (approx.)

WHY THIS STEP? The minor sector PLUS the major sector cover the entire disc. So subtracting the minor sector area from the full disc area πr² leaves precisely the major sector area.

Method B - ‘Use the major-sector angle directly’ (faded - you complete the last simplification):
Alternatively, area of the major sector = ((360 - θ)/360) × πr²
= ((360 - 30)/360) × 3.14 × 16 cm²
= (330/360) × 3.14 × 16 cm² = 46.05 cm²
= 46.1 cm² (approx.)

Notice that Method A and Method B agree to the rounding precision - a powerful self-check whenever you have time for both.

ERROR ALERT: A common slip is to use θ = 30 in the major-sector formula - forgetting that the major sector’s own angle is 360° - 30° = 330°. The phrase ‘corresponding major sector’ means ‘the OTHER sector’, not the same one.

CHECK: Suppose the problem changed to radius 4 cm and central angle 45°. (a) Compute the minor sector area using π = 3.14. (b) Then state the major sector area in two ways - via Method A and via Method B - and verify they agree to two decimal places.

carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: The previous worked example used only the sector formula. The next problem is harder: it asks for a SEGMENT area at an angle of 120°. Because the angle is not 90°, the inscribed isosceles triangle’s area cannot be read off as (1/2) × base × height directly. We will need a perpendicular construction plus the trigonometric ratios sin 60° and cos 60° from your earlier classes.

RECALL: Area of a segment = Area of the corresponding sector - Area of Δ OAB. We have the sector formula and we know how to set up an isosceles triangle from a chord; trigonometry will provide the missing side lengths.

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 (complete):
Example 2 : Find the area of the segment AYB shown in Fig. 11.6, if radius of the circle is 21 cm and ∠ AOB = 120°. (Use π = 22/7)

Solution : Area of the segment AYB
= Area of sector OAYB - Area of Δ OAB     … (1)

Step 1 - Compute the sector area:
Now, area of the sector OAYB = (120/360) × (22/7) × 21 × 21 cm² = 462 cm²     … (2)

WHY THIS STEP? Substitute θ = 120, r = 21, and notice 120/360 = 1/3, while (22/7) × 21 × 21 = 22 × 3 × 21 = 1386. One-third of 1386 is 462. Calculations with π = 22/7 work out cleanly when r is a multiple of 7.

Step 2 - Set up the triangle by dropping a perpendicular:
For finding the area of Δ OAB, draw OM ⊥ AB as shown in Fig. 11.7.
Note that OA = OB. Therefore, by RHS congruence, Δ AMO ≅ Δ BMO.
So, M is the mid-point of AB and ∠ AOM = ∠ BOM = (1/2) × 120° = 60°.

WHY THIS STEP? OA = OB because both are radii. The perpendicular from the apex of an isosceles triangle to the base bisects both the base AND the apex angle - so each half-angle is 60°, and we now have two right triangles with a 60° angle.

Step 3 - Use cosine to find OM:
Let OM = x cm
So, from Δ OMA, OM / OA = cos 60°
or, x / 21 = 1/2     [cos 60° = 1/2]
or, x = 21/2

So, OM = 21/2 cm

Step 4 - Use sine to find AM, hence AB:
Also, AM / OA = sin 60° = √3 / 2
So, AM = (21√3) / 2 cm
Therefore, AB = 2 AM = 2 × (21√3)/2 cm = 21√3 cm

Step 5 - Triangle area, then segment area:
So, area of Δ OAB = (1/2) × AB × OM = (1/2) × 21√3 × (21/2) cm²
= (441√3) / 4 cm²     … (3)

Therefore, area of the segment AYB = (462 - (441√3)/4) cm²     [From (1), (2) and (3)]
= (21/4) (88 - 21√3) cm²

WHY THIS STEP? We left the answer in exact (surd) form because √3 is irrational. Substituting √3 ≈ 1.732 and rounding can be done if the question asks for a numerical answer; otherwise the exact form is preferred.

ERROR ALERT: A common slip is to forget the half-angle - students apply sin 120° to the original triangle directly. The cleaner route is to drop the perpendicular and work with the half-angle (60° here) inside a right triangle, where sin and cos are unambiguous.

HOOK: You have the formulas, you have seen them at work in two examples. Time to use them on the official exercise. The first four questions check four different applications of the same two ideas - sector area and chord-formed segment - with a small twist in each. Read carefully before substituting; the trick is often in how the central angle is hidden in the wording.

EXERCISE 11.1

Unless stated otherwise, use π = 22/7.

1. Find the area of a sector of a circle with radius 6 cm if angle of the sector is 60°.

WHAT’S THE SITUATION?: A standard sector area question. Both r and θ are stated explicitly. Substitute and simplify.

2. Find the area of a quadrant of a circle whose circumference is 22 cm.

WHAT’S THE SITUATION?: A quadrant is a quarter of a circle, so its central angle is 90°. The catch is that you are given the circumference, not the radius. WHAT DO WE KNOW?: 2πr = 22 cm. TRANSLATE TO MATHS: First find r from 2πr = 22, then apply Area = (90/360) × πr².

3. The length of the minute hand of a clock is 14 cm. Find the area swept by the minute hand in 5 minutes.

WHAT’S THE SITUATION?: The minute hand sweeps a sector as it moves. WHAT DO WE KNOW?: r = 14 cm; in 60 minutes the hand sweeps 360°, so in 5 minutes it sweeps (5/60) × 360° = 30°. TRANSLATE TO MATHS: Area = (30/360) × πr².

4. A chord of a circle of radius 10 cm subtends a right angle at the centre. Find the area of the corresponding : (i) minor segment (ii) major sector. (Use π = 3.14)

WHAT’S THE SITUATION?: θ = 90°, r = 10 cm. The chord-and-two-radii triangle is right-angled at O with both legs equal to r, so its area is straightforward. (i) Minor segment = sector area - triangle area. (ii) Major sector = πr² - minor sector area.

WHY THESE STEPS? Each problem has the SAME core formula but a DIFFERENT cover story. Q1 hands you both inputs; Q2 hides r inside the circumference; Q3 hides θ inside time; Q4 asks you to combine sector and triangle. Your job in PRACTICE is to translate first, then compute.

ERROR ALERT: In Q3, students sometimes treat ‘5 minutes’ as if it were 5° of angle. Always convert: full sweep is 360° in 60 minutes, so each minute is 6°, and 5 minutes is 30°.

CHECK: Without computing actual numbers, predict for each question (a) which formula(s) you need, (b) what the angle in degrees is, and (c) what units the final answer carries. Then carry out Q1 to a numerical answer using π = 22/7.

5. In a circle of radius 21 cm, an arc subtends an angle of 60° at the centre. Find:
   (i) the length of the arc
   (ii) area of the sector formed by the arc
   (iii) area of the segment formed by the corresponding chord

WHAT’S THE SITUATION?: Three sub-questions, one shared setup. WHAT DO WE KNOW?: r = 21 cm, θ = 60°. TRANSLATE TO MATHS: (i) Arc length = (60/360) × 2πr. (ii) Sector area = (60/360) × πr². 6. A chord of a circle of radius 15 cm subtends an angle of 60° at the centre. Find the areas of the corresponding minor and major segments of the circle. (Use π = 3.14 and √3 = 1.73)

WHAT’S THE SITUATION?: r = 15 cm, θ = 60°. WHAT DO WE WANT TO FIND?: Both minor and major segment areas. TRANSLATE TO MATHS: Minor segment = sector area - triangle area. Major segment = πr² - minor segment.

WHAT’S THE SITUATION?: θ = 120°, so the triangle is NOT equilateral. Drop OM ⊥ AB exactly as in Worked Example 2; the half-angle is 60°; use sin 60° and cos 60° to get AB and OM, then the triangle area, then subtract from the sector area.

WHY THESE STEPS? Q5 and Q6 with θ = 60° give equilateral triangles - one shortcut. Q7 with θ = 120° needs the perpendicular construction. Recognising the angle BEFORE you start choosing your triangle method saves time.

ERROR ALERT: For θ = 60°, students sometimes still drop the perpendicular and grind through sin 30° and cos 30°. Correct - but slower than just using the equilateral shortcut: if all three sides equal r, then triangle area = (√3 / 4) r².

8. A horse is tied to a peg at one corner of a square shaped grass field of side 15 m by means of a 5 m long rope (see Fig. 11.8). Find
   (i) the area of that part of the field in which the horse can graze.
   (ii) the increase in the grazing area if the rope were 10 m long instead of 5 m. (Use π = 3.14)

WHAT’S THE SITUATION?: A horse tethered at a corner can swing the rope inside a quarter-circle (the two field walls block the other three quarters). For (ii), the longer rope swings inside a larger quarter-circle.

WHAT DO WE KNOW?: Field is a 15 m × 15 m square. Rope length r = 5 m, then r = 10 m. The rope length is the radius of the rope’s circle. The corner forces the central angle to 90° because two perpendicular walls meet there.

WHAT DO WE WANT TO FIND?: (i) Area of the quarter-circle of radius 5 m. (ii) The DIFFERENCE between a quarter-circle of radius 10 m and a quarter-circle of radius 5 m - not the area of the bigger one alone.

TRANSLATE TO MATHS:
(i) Grazing area = (90/360) × πr² = (1/4) × 3.14 × 5 × 5 m².
(ii) Increase = (1/4) × 3.14 × 10 × 10 m² - (1/4) × 3.14 × 5 × 5 m².

WHY THIS STEP? When the rope length doubles, the radius doubles, but the area scales as radius-squared - it quadruples, not doubles. The new grazing area is FOUR times the old, so the INCREASE is three times the original.

ERROR ALERT: A common mistake is to read ‘increase’ as the new total area. Re-read the question - it asks for the difference (extra area gained), so subtract the old grazing area from the new one. Another slip is to assume the horse can graze a full circle around the peg; the field walls at the corner restrict the sweep to exactly one quarter.

ALSO BEWARE - A SIDE-LENGTH CONSTRAINT: For (ii), the rope is 10 m and the field side is 15 m. Because 10 < 15, the rope still does not reach the opposite walls, so the quarter-circle approximation is still valid. If the rope had been longer than the side, the geometry would have become more complicated.

CHECK: After computing both grazing areas, verify your ‘increase’ by comparing it with 3 times the original grazing area. They should match exactly when the area scales as r².

Given: rope length r = 5 m, square field of side 15 m, π = 3.14.
Grazing region = quarter-circle of radius 5 m, so central angle = 90°.
Formula: Grazing area = (90/360) × πr² = (1/4) × 3.14 × 5 × 5 m².
Calculation: (1/4) × 3.14 × 25 = 78.5 / 4 = 19.625 m².
Result: Grazing area = 19.625 m².
recall_questions.prompt: For Q8, compute the grazing area when the rope is 5 m long, using π = 3.14. Show each step.

recall_questions.answer:
The error is treating area as a linear function of r. Area scales as r², not r.
Correct: when r doubles from 5 m to 10 m, the area increases by a factor of 2² = 4.
Check: original area = (1/4) × 3.14 × 25 = 19.625 m²; new area = (1/4) × 3.14 × 100 = 78.5 m²; ratio = 78.5 / 19.625 = 4. Doubling r quadruples the area.

9. A brooch is made with silver wire in the form of a circle with diameter 35 mm. The wire is also used in making 5 diameters which divide the circle into 10 equal sectors as shown in Fig. 11.9. Find :
   (i) the total length of the silver wire required.
   (ii) the area of each sector of the brooch.

WHAT’S THE SITUATION?: A circular wire frame plus 5 straight diameters across it. Each diameter passes through the centre and crosses the boundary at two points; together they cut the disc into 10 equal sector-wedges.

WHAT DO WE KNOW?: Diameter = 35 mm, so radius r = 35/2 mm = 17.5 mm. Number of sectors = 10. Central angle per sector θ = 360° ÷ 10 = 36°.

TRANSLATE TO MATHS:
(i) Total wire = (circumference) + (5 diameters) = 2πr + 5 × 35 mm.
(ii) Each sector area = (36/360) × πr² = (1/10) × π × (17.5)² mm².

10. An umbrella has 8 ribs which are equally spaced (see Fig. 11.10). Assuming umbrella to be a flat circle of radius 45 cm, find the area between the two consecutive ribs of the umbrella.

WHAT’S THE SITUATION?: An umbrella laid flat as a 45 cm-radius circle, with 8 ribs cutting it into 8 equal sector slices.

TRANSLATE TO MATHS: Central angle per sector = 360° ÷ 8 = 45°. Area between two consecutive ribs = (45/360) × πr² with r = 45 cm.

11. A car has two wipers which do not overlap. Each wiper has a blade of length 25 cm sweeping through an angle of 115°. Find the total area cleaned at each sweep of the blades.

WHAT’S THE SITUATION?: Each wiper traces out a single sector. Two wipers, no overlap, so total cleaned area = 2 × (one wiper’s sector area).

TRANSLATE TO MATHS: Total area = 2 × (115/360) × π × 25 × 25 cm².

WHY THESE STEPS? In Q9 and Q10, the central angle is HIDDEN - you must derive it from the count of equal sectors. In Q11, the central angle is given directly, and the only twist is the ‘two wipers, no overlap’ multiplication. Recognising whether θ is given or derived is the strategy step.

ERROR ALERT: For Q9, students sometimes count ‘five diameters’ as five sectors. But each diameter is a straight line passing through the centre, which actually creates two cuts - so 5 diameters yield 10 sectors. For Q11, do NOT add the angles 115° + 115° = 230° and put it into one formula - that would only be valid if the two wipers shared a common pivot, which they do not.

CHECK (faded): For Q10, after you compute the area between two consecutive ribs, multiply your answer by 8 and confirm it equals πr² with r = 45 cm. Why must this product be exactly the area of the full umbrella?

recall_questions.prompt: Why does a brooch with 5 diameters drawn through the centre divide the disc into 10 equal sectors and not 5?

recall_questions.answer:
Given: r = 45 cm, 8 equally spaced ribs, π = 22/7.
Central angle per sector θ = 360° ÷ 8 = 45°.
Area between two consecutive ribs = (45/360) × πr² = (1/8) × (22/7) × 45 × 45 cm².
Calculation: (1/8) × (22/7) × 2025 = (22 × 2025) / 56 = 44550 / 56 ≈ 795.54 cm².
Result: Area between two consecutive ribs ≈ 795.54 cm².
recall_questions.prompt: For Q10 (umbrella with 8 ribs, r = 45 cm, π = 22/7), find the area between two consecutive ribs of the umbrella. Show each step.

recall_questions.answer:
Each wiper has its OWN pivot (the wipers do not share a common centre). So each wiper traces its own independent sector of central angle 115° and radius 25 cm.

12. To warn ships for underwater rocks, a lighthouse spreads a red coloured light over a sector of angle 80° to a distance of 16.5 km. Find the area of the sea over which the ships are warned. (Use π = 3.14)

WHAT’S THE SITUATION?: A lighthouse standing at the centre projects light outward in a fan-shape. The fan IS a sector of a circle of radius 16.5 km, with central angle 80°.

TRANSLATE TO MATHS: Warned area = (80/360) × πr² with r = 16.5 km. Final unit will be km².

13. A round table cover has six equal designs as shown in Fig. 11.11. If the radius of the cover is 28 cm, find the cost of making the designs at the rate of ₹ 0.35 per cm². (Use √3 = 1.7)

WHAT’S THE SITUATION?: A 28 cm-radius circle has six equal segment-shaped designs around its rim. Each design is a SEGMENT - the sliver between a chord and an arc - not a sector. The chord of each segment subtends a central angle of 360° ÷ 6 = 60°. The triangle formed by the chord and the two radii is therefore equilateral (θ = 60° means all three sides equal r).

TRANSLATE TO MATHS:
Step 1 - One segment area = sector area - triangle area = ((60/360) × πr²) - ((√3 / 4) r²) with r = 28 cm.
Step 2 - Total design area = 6 × (one segment area).
Step 3 - Cost = total area × ₹ 0.35 per cm².

WHY THIS STEP? The equilateral-triangle area shortcut (√3 / 4) r² saves you from setting up sin and cos again. It works only because θ = 60° forces all three sides of the inscribed triangle to be equal to the radius.

14. Tick the correct answer in the following :
Area of a sector of angle p (in degrees) of a circle with radius R is
(A) (p/180) × 2πR
(B) (p/180) × πR²
(C) (p/360) × 2πR
(D) (p/720) × 2πR²

WHAT’S THE SITUATION?: A multiple-choice check on the very first formula you derived in this chapter. Compare each option with the standard form (p/360) × πR².

WHY THIS STEP? Option (B) is wrong because the denominator should be 360, not 180. Option (C) is the arc-length formula, not the area formula. Option (D) can be re-written: (p/720) × 2πR² = (p/360) × πR² - exactly the sector area formula. So (D) is the correct answer.

ERROR ALERT: A common slip in Q13 is to forget that the design is a segment, not a sector - leading to a much larger (sector area only) answer. Always check whether the figure shows a chord-bounded sliver (segment) or a wedge from the centre (sector).

11.2 Summary

In this chapter, you have studied the following points :

1. Length of an arc of a sector of a circle with radius r and angle with degree measure θ is (θ/360) × 2πr

This is the same arc length you used to compute the curved part of the cricket boundary (Topic M1.S2.T3) and the arc in Q5 of the exercise.

2. Area of a sector of a circle with radius r and angle with degree measure θ is (θ/360) × πr²

This is the workhorse formula. It powered the Diwali rangoli wedge in M1.S2.T2, both methods of Worked Example 1, the minute-hand sweep in Q3, the umbrella slice in Q10, the wiper sweep in Q11, the lighthouse fan in Q12, and the brooch in Q9.

3. Area of segment of a circle = Area of the corresponding sector - Area of the corresponding triangle.

This is the segment formula in its general form. It powered Worked Example 2 (with sin/cos at θ = 120°), Q4 (right-angle triangle at θ = 90°), Q5-Q7 (varied θ with chords), and the six equilateral-triangle segments of the round table in Q13.

WHY THIS STEP? Notice that the SAME factor (θ/360) controls both the arc length and the sector area. The segment formula then uses the sector area as one ingredient and subtracts a triangle. So all three results are stacked on the same Unitary-Method idea - ‘the central angle is the fraction of the full circle’.

ERROR ALERT: When a question asks for a major sector or major segment, do not push θ directly into the formula - think ‘(360 - θ)’ instead, or use the ‘full disc minus minor region’ identity (πr² - minor area). When a question asks for a segment, never forget to SUBTRACT the triangle from the sector.

CHECK: In one sentence each, state (a) the factor common to all three formulas, (b) the difference between sector area and segment area, and (c) the correct way to find a major sector area from a known minor sector area.
